Propensity scores include only age, PSA, and Charlson Comorbidity Index, while crucial determinants of prognosis and prescribing are unavailable or omitted, including metastatic status, disease volume, Gleason grade, stage, castration-sensitive vs castration-resistant status, testosterone, performance status, diabetes duration and severity, body mass index, and indication for SGLT2 inhibitor use. Prior treatment is not a sufficient proxy for stage. Given the small exposed sample and strong confounding by both cancer severity and metabolic health, the reported associations cannot presently support causal or adjunctive-treatment claims.
- The handling of covariates is insufficiently justified. Numerous laboratory values and medications are updated during follow-up and included in outcome models, but some may be affected by SGLT2 inhibitor treatment and therefore represent mediators or colliders. The manuscript should distinguish baseline from time-varying confounders, specify the causal model motivating adjustment, report missingness and imputation procedures, and avoid adjustment for postexposure variables without an appropriate longitudinal causal method.
- Matching and balance reporting are inadequate. Table 1 shows only 3 variables, with residual standardized mean differences of 0.12 and 0.16 after matching; balance for the many other prognostic factors used later is not shown. The manuscript should report balance across all measured confounders, matching quality by sequential trial, the number of unique patients and replicated trial records, discarded initiators, and overlap/positivity diagnostics.
- The primary outcome combines a laboratory progression definition with treatment initiation. NHA initiation is influenced by calendar period, access, clinician preference, comorbidity, and evolving standards of care across this exceptionally long study period. The PSA definition and confirmation interval should be justified against accepted prostate cancer progression criteria. Analyses separating biochemical progression from NHA initiation are needed.
- Death is a substantial competing event in this elderly cohort, with 44.4% overall mortality. For ADT and NHA failure, censoring death and estimating Kaplan-Meier–type cumulative risks may overestimate event probabilities. The estimand for competing death should be specified and cumulative incidence estimated accordingly. The source and validity of prostate cancer–specific cause of death should also be reported.
- The estimates are based on only 159 SGLT2 inhibitor users and 44 exposed patients in the NHA analysis, with wide confidence intervals and borderline P values. Ten-year absolute risks may rely on sparse or absent support because SGLT2 inhibitors entered practice relatively recently. Numbers at risk, exposure-era distributions, median follow-up among initiators, and uncertainty around absolute risk reductions and numbers needed to treat are essential. Extrapolated estimates beyond adequately supported follow-up should not be presented.
- Multiple outcomes, comparator definitions, estimands, drug comparisons, and sensitivity analyses are tested without a clear multiplicity strategy. Several conclusions rely on marginal P values, and the statement that conventional Cox models “confirmed robust associations across all outcomes” appears inconsistent with the nonsignificant survival results presented. The findings should be framed as exploratory, emphasizing effect sizes and uncertainty rather than statistical significance.
- The interpretation overreaches the data. Comparisons with nondiabetic patients do not isolate an SGLT2-specific anticancer effect, and a null metformin association does not establish a nonglycemic mechanism. The conclusion that class-wide anticancer effects are consistent is unsupported by an underpowered dapagliflozin-vs-empagliflozin comparison, especially when the cited preclinical evidence suggests drug-specific differences.

MINOR CONCERNS:
- Provide the complete target trial protocol in the main manuscript or summarize all key components there; reliance on an unavailable supplement prevents assessment of the emulation.
- Clarify whether Table 1 reports unique individuals or person-trial records and why the DSS and OS sample counts differ from the primary matched cohort.
- Report event counts by treatment group for every analysis rather than only total sample sizes.
- Replace baseline hypothesis-testing P values with standardized differences; baseline significance testing after matching is not informative.
- Correct “A -sided P < .05” to “A 2-sided P < .05.”
- The reference numbering is malformed around references 13 and 14.
- Use consistent terminology for “patients without diabetes” rather than “nondiabetic,” and distinguish absence of glucose-lowering medication from confirmed absence of diabetes.
- Avoid post hoc power calculations, which add little beyond the confidence intervals.
- Temper mechanistic discussion and reduce repetition regarding metformin and purported glucose-independent effects.
- Describe prescription exposure in sufficient detail, including dose, adherence assumptions, inpatient/outpatient capture, and handling of stockpiling.
- State how last hospital contact was determined and whether loss to follow-up differed by treatment strategy.
- Explain ascertainment and validation of ADT duration, PSA measurements, progression dates, and cause-specific mortality in the electronic record.

DECISION: reject

SUMMARY:
This population-based cohort study using Swedish registry data examines the association between quadrivalent HPV vaccination and incidence of high-grade vulvovaginal lesions. The authors report that vaccinated women had lower incidence of high-grade vulvovaginal lesions compared to unvaccinated women, with the strongest protection observed among those vaccinated at ages 10-16 years, and that birth cohorts eligible for subsidized or catch-up vaccination programs showed population-level reductions in lesion incidence.

MAJOR CONCERNS:
1. The manuscript appears to be incomplete and contains numerous formatting errors and duplicated text. The Methods section is truncated with placeholder text ("[…]"), and key methodological details are missing. The Results section similarly contains incomplete sentences and missing data. This manuscript is not in a reviewable state.

2. The outcome definition combines high-grade vulvar lesions, vulvar cancer, high-grade vaginal lesions, and vaginal cancer into a single composite outcome. These are clinically distinct entities with different etiologies and natural histories. The authors should justify this composite and also present results separately given the known stronger association of HPV with certain lesion types.

3. The primary analysis treats vaccination as a time-varying exposure with no buffer period, yet the authors acknowledge that prevalent infections at vaccination could bias results. While sensitivity analyses with 1- and 2-year buffer periods are mentioned, these are relegated to supplementary material. Given that the primary analysis fails to show statistically significant protection for the 17+ age group while buffer-period analyses do show significant effects, the choice of primary analysis approach requires stronger justification.

4. The birth cohort analysis comparing opportunistic (1985-1988), subsidized (1989-1992), and catch-up (1993-1998) cohorts is confounded by age. Since older cohorts have had longer follow-up and more time to develop lesions, the observed "population-level reduction" may simply reflect age differences rather than vaccination program effects. The authors should provide age-standardized rates or otherwise address this confounding.

5. The authors state that women vaccinated at 17 years or older showed reduced incidence but "the difference was not statistically significant" in the primary analysis, yet later claim that with buffer periods, significant reductions were observed. This selective emphasis on favorable sensitivity analyses while downplaying null primary results is problematic.

6. The Methods section mentions adjustment for "parental education level, annual household income, and parental history of HPV-related precancers and cancers," but it is unclear how these covariates were measured and whether they were time-varying. More detail on covariate assessment is needed.

7. The authors note that "certain high-grade vulvovaginal lesions... could be detected through cervical screening or gynecological examinations" and that vaccinated women may be more likely to attend screening. However, they do not appear to account for screening participation in their models, which could introduce detection bias.

8. The manuscript lacks a formal assessment of the proportional hazards assumption for the Cox models, which is critical for the validity of the reported hazard ratios.

MINOR CONCERNS:
1. The introduction repeats the same information multiple times, suggesting incomplete editing.

2. The Discussion section overstates the strength of evidence for "catch-up" vaccination programs given the confounding issues noted above.

3. The authors mention that "there were 4 outcomes before age 17 years in the unvaccinated group, 1 in those vaccinated at 10 to 16 years, and 0 in those vaccinated at 17 years or older" but do not explain the relevance of this observation clearly.

4. The reference list appears incomplete, with several references cited in text but not listed.

5. The manuscript lacks a clear statement on patient and public involvement in the research.

6. Table 1 and Figure 2 are referenced but their content is not fully described in the text.

7. The authors should clarify whether the Swedish HPV vaccination register (SVEVAC) captures all doses administered, including those given in private settings.

DECISION: reject

The manuscript in its current form is incomplete and not suitable for peer review. The research question is important and the registry-based approach has merit, but the analysis has methodological concerns including potential age confounding in the birth cohort analysis, detection bias from differential screening, and selective reporting of sensitivity analyses. The authors should substantially revise the manuscript to address these issues before resubmission.

SUMMARY:
This nationwide population-based cohort study of 67,390 Danish females evaluated whether undergoing a first-trimester medication or procedural abortion was associated with subsequent risks of first-time psychotropic medication redemptions compared with the pre-abortion period (1 year prior). While modest increases in first-time psychotropic and antianxiety medication redemptions were observed in the first year post-abortion under nominal alpha levels (P < .05), these associations largely attenuated and were non-significant after Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons, with long-term follow-up (>5 years) showing lower rates of medication redemption. The authors conclude that the data do not support claims of substantial or sustained negative mental health sequelae attributable to medication or procedural abortion.

MAJOR CONCERNS:
None.

MINOR CONCERNS:
1. In the fully adjusted model (Table 3), the increased risk for antianxiety medication redemption 2 to 5 years following medication abortion (IRR, 1.26; 95% CI, 1.11–1.44; P < .001) remains statistically significant even after Bonferroni correction. While the authors discuss this in the context of the 8-week gestational age sensitivity analysis, please provide a brief clinical or methodological discussion regarding potential mechanisms or residual confounding driving this isolated signal.
2. In the Methods section under "Study Population", it states "Analyses were conducted between June 2023 and June 2025." Please verify and update the completion date to reflect actual analysis timing.
3. In Table 1, under "Father's presence during childhood", check the percentage and sample counts to ensure consistent alignment with the narrative and other registry-linked variables.

DECISION: minor_revision

**Reviewer Comments — Manuscript: "Lymph Node Dissection Guideline Adherence and Survival in Patients With T1N0M0 Lung Adenocarcinoma"**

SUMMARY: The authors analyzed 27,191 patients with cT1N0M0 lung adenocarcinoma from a 19-center Chinese EHR database (NCC LungReal), categorizing tumors as lepidic-without-high-grade (LepNH) or high-grade-or-no-lepidic (HGNL). They report that guideline-adherent lymph node dissection (3+1 or 6-station standard) was associated with improved overall survival in the HGNL group but not in the LepNH group, and provide lobe/size/pattern-specific nodal involvement rates, concluding that the extent of dissection might be tailored to histologic pattern.

MAJOR CONCERNS:

1. **Confounding by indication is severe and only partially addressable.** The nonadherent groups had smaller tumors, more wedge/segmentectomy, fewer stations and nodes examined, and lower pathologic upstaging. Surgeons likely selected limited dissection for patients perceived as low-risk (small ground-glass lesions, poor reserve, etc.). The authors acknowledge this in the Limitations, but the core conclusion—that adherence itself confers survival benefit in HGNL tumors—rests on an assumption that surgeon judgment is fully captured by the adjusted covariates. The E-values reported (1.78–2.67) are modest and easily explained by plausible unmeasured confounding. This should be stated more prominently, including in the Abstract/Key Points, not only in the Discussion.

2. **Stage-migration and adjuvant-therapy mediation.** More extensive dissection detects more node-positive disease (10.2% vs 5.7% pN1-2), which can direct adjuvant therapy and improve survival. The survival benefit of "adherence" may therefore be mediated largely by accurate staging and subsequent treatment rather than by the dissection itself. The authors lack adjuvant therapy data (acknowledged), but this alternative explanation deserves explicit discussion and should temper the causal framing of the Key Points ("Meaning").

3. **Post-treatment variable used to define analysis groups.** Histologic pattern (LepNH vs HGNL) is only known definitively after resection and complete pathologic evaluation. Conditioning on final histology may introduce collider bias and limits the clinical actionability of the findings (intraoperative frozen section sensitivity for high-grade patterns is only 37%–69%, as the authors themselves note). The practical message—that one can omit dissection in LepNH tumors—cannot be operationalized reliably with current intraoperative assessment; this tension should be addressed directly.

4. **Underpowered and internally inconsistent subgroup findings.** The median follow-up is only 24.9 months with 798 deaths (2.9%), and many subgroup analyses have EPV <10 (appropriately flagged as exploratory). Notably, the 3+1 benefit appears in the 1–2 cm subgroup while the 6-station benefit appears only in the 2–3 cm subgroup—a pattern that could readily reflect chance, and the biologic rationale for this discordance is not explained. The LepNH "no benefit" conclusion is based on only 139 events and wide CIs (e.g., 6-station HR 0.54, 95% CI 0.26–1.13); absence of evidence should not be presented as evidence of absence with equal rhetorical weight.

5. **Questionable adequacy of clinical staging.** Only ~9% of patients underwent PET-CT within 90 days preoperatively. For a study of cN0 patients comparing nodal dissection strategies, the clinical N0 determination is central; reliance largely on CT alone raises concern about misclassification that may differ by center and era. Please clarify how clinical N status was established and perform sensitivity analyses restricted to PET-staged patients.

6. **Overlapping comparison groups.** Most 6-station–adherent patients are also 3+1-adherent. The comparison of "6-station vs only 3+1" is informative, but the two primary analyses (3+1 adherent vs nonadherent; 6-station adherent vs nonadherent) share patients and are not independent; this should be stated and the correlated nature of the tests acknowledged.

7. **Generalizability.** The cohort is entirely from Chinese centers with a high proportion of never-smokers and, presumably, many screen-detected subsolid lesions. Generalizability to Western populations should be explicitly qualified.

MINOR CONCERNS:

- Abstract Key Points should note the modest absolute benefit (~1 percentage point; NNT ~80–100) and the observational nature more prominently.
- Introduction: "associated the 3 + 1 standard" — missing "with"; "remain unclear" → "remains unclear."
- Table: pathology T2/T3-4 in a clinically T1 cohort deserves comment (measurement vs upstaging discrepancy).
- The registration number (NCT06255197) postdates the study period; clarify that registration was retrospective.
- Figure 1 legend: "Lipidic" should be "Lepidic"; clarify why stations 3, 13, 14 are excluded.
- The claim "largest analysis to our knowledge" should be supported or hedged.
- Consider reporting recurrence-free survival if any proxy data exist, or state its unavailability earlier.
- Numbers needed to treat are given in Discussion text but not in Results; move or report consistently.

DECISION: major_revision

SUMMARY: This multicenter retrospective cohort study of 27 191 patients with resected cT1N0M0 lung adenocarcinoma reports that adherence to either the 3 + 1 or 6-station lymph node assessment standard was associated with modestly better overall survival among tumors classified as high-grade or lacking a lepidic pattern, but not among tumors with lepidic and no high-grade patterns. The authors also report substantially greater nodal involvement in the former histologic group and propose histology-informed tailoring of nodal assessment.

MAJOR CONCERNS:
- The central inference is highly vulnerable to residual confounding. Patients receiving less extensive nodal assessment were more likely to undergo wedge resection or segmentectomy, and the database apparently lacks comorbidity, performance status, pulmonary function, frailty, surgeon-level factors, detailed imaging characteristics, and reasons for limited dissection. These factors strongly influence both surgical management and overall survival. Adjustment, weighting, and modest E-values do not resolve this concern; the observed absolute survival differences of approximately 1 percentage point could plausibly be explained by such confounding. The manuscript should avoid “survival benefit” terminology throughout and characterize the findings strictly as noncausal associations.
- The proposed stratification variable is derived from the final resection specimen and therefore generally is not available when nodal dissection is performed. Frozen-section sensitivity for high-grade patterns is acknowledged to be poor. More importantly, the broad HGNL category combines tumors with any amount of a high-grade component with tumors having no lepidic component, without reporting pattern percentages or predominant subtype. This heterogeneous, postoperative classifier has limited immediate clinical utility. Analyses using predominant subtype, prespecified percentage thresholds, and variables potentially available preoperatively or intraoperatively would be more informative.
- A differential association by histologic group cannot be established by finding statistical significance in HGNL and nonsignificance in LepNH. A formal adherence-by-histologic-group interaction test is required for each nodal standard, with presentation of interaction estimates and confidence intervals. Given only 139 deaths in the LepNH group, the study has limited power to exclude a clinically meaningful association there; the conclusion that no benefit exists in this group is too strong.
- Follow-up is immature for an early-stage population: median follow-up among survivors was only 24.9 months, only 798 deaths occurred, and 3-year survival was exceptionally high. The manuscript repeatedly refers to “long-term survival,” which is not supported. Numbers at risk at 3 years, completeness of follow-up by center and exposure group, reverse Kaplan-Meier follow-up estimates, and proportional-hazards diagnostics should be provided. Longer follow-up and recurrence outcomes would be substantially more suitable for this question.
- Clinical staging appears heterogeneous and potentially inadequate: only approximately 9% underwent PET-CT within 90 days, and data on endobronchial ultrasonography or mediastinoscopy were unavailable. The authors should explain precisely how cN0 and cT1 status were assigned across centers, whether PET-CT performed outside the 90-day definition was captured, and whether radiographic solid-component or invasive size was used. Differential preoperative staging could affect both the choice of nodal assessment and outcomes.
- Station-specific involvement rates use the number of patients in whom a station was examined as the denominator. Because stations were selected for examination nonrandomly, these estimates are subject to verification and selection bias and should not be interpreted as population-level risks of station involvement. Likewise, the greater pathologic nodal upstaging with guideline adherence is partly a mechanical consequence of more complete ascertainment. These analyses require clearer qualification and, if possible, adjustment for factors determining station selection.
- Histologic classification reliability needs clarification. The manuscript does not state whether specimens underwent central pathology review, whether all centers used common definitions and minimum percentage thresholds, or how interobserver variability—particularly for complex glandular and cribriform patterns—was addressed. Excluding all patients without pattern data may also introduce selection bias; counts and characteristics of these exclusions should be reported.
- The two adherence definitions are nested, and numerous subgroup and comparative analyses are presented. The statistical hierarchy and multiplicity strategy require clearer specification. Size-stratified and 6-station-vs-3 + 1 findings, especially those based on sparse events and marginal P values, should be explicitly labeled hypothesis-generating and not used to recommend one standard over another.

MINOR CONCERNS:
- Use “lymph node assessment” rather than “dissection” when adherence is defined only by stations examined; the data do not necessarily establish the operative technique or completeness of removal.
- Report cause-specific mortality if available. Overall survival is particularly susceptible to differences in baseline health and competing mortality.
- Clarify how absolute risk differences and numbers needed to treat were estimated from adjusted observational models. “Number needed to treat” implies causality and should preferably be replaced by an adjusted absolute survival difference.
- Provide distributions of follow-up and deaths by histologic group, size subgroup, adherence group, and center, as well as effective sample sizes after weighting.
- Explain the handling of missing data more fully, including which variables were imputed, percentages missing, number of imputations, and whether outcomes or exposure variables were imputed.
- The manuscript should report postoperative treatment by nodal stage if obtainable. Accurate upstaging and subsequent adjuvant therapy are proposed mechanisms, but adjuvant treatment data are absent.
- Correct typographic and grammatical issues, including “Lipidic” to “Lepidic” in Figure 1, “associated the 3 + 1 standard” to “associated with,” “remain unclear” to “remains unclear,” and the missing closing parenthesis in the Figure 1 citation.
- The title and Key Points should explicitly identify the study as observational and avoid implying that histology-guided omission of guideline-adherent nodal assessment has been established as safe.

DECISION: major_revision

SUMMARY: This report presents approximately 5-year follow-up of the randomized, double-blind CAPTAIN-1st trial, finding longer overall survival with first-line camrelizumab plus gemcitabine-cisplatin than with placebo plus chemotherapy in Chinese patients with recurrent or metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma. It also reports exploratory associations between early plasma Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) DNA clearance and long-term survival.

MAJOR CONCERNS:
- The inferential status of the OS result requires substantial clarification and more cautious interpretation. Although OS was a key secondary end point, no hierarchical testing or multiplicity adjustment was prespecified, and the manuscript calls the current analysis “post hoc.” The unadjusted result is borderline (HR, 0.74; 95% CI, 0.55-0.99; P = .047), making the lack of multiplicity control consequential. The protocol and statistical analysis plan should identify whether this cutoff, number of events, and analysis were prespecified. If not, the OS findings should be consistently characterized as nominal or exploratory, including in the Abstract, Key Points, Discussion, and Conclusions; claims that the analysis “demonstrated” benefit or establishes a standard of care should be tempered.
- Long-term follow-up completeness needs fuller accounting. Twenty-one patients were lost to follow-up, and the discrepancy between the Kaplan-Meier 5-year estimates and the proportions identified as confirmed 5-year survivors is material, particularly in the camrelizumab group (37.8% vs 32.1%). Please provide numbers at risk and censoring distributions near 60 months, dates of last contact for those lost, and sensitivity analyses assessing informative censoring. The designation “final” should also be justified given 68% event maturity and the number lost to follow-up.
- The age-adjusted analysis appears data-driven: age imbalance and its prognostic association were identified after randomization, after which adjustment strengthened the HR from 0.74 to 0.65 and the P value from .047 to .006. This should be explicitly labeled post hoc and presented only as a sensitivity analysis, not as “further strengthening” the primary evidence. Age should preferably be modeled continuously, with rationale for any cutoff; the inconsistent categories (<50/≥50 in the Table and ≤50/>50 in the subgroup analysis) must be corrected.
- The EBV DNA analyses are vulnerable to guarantee-time/immortal-time and selection biases because clearance during the first 3 cycles is a postbaseline variable, yet OS appears to be measured from randomization. A prespecified landmark analysis after cycle 3, restricted to patients alive and under observation at that time, or an appropriate time-dependent Cox model is needed. The authors should account for patients lacking evaluable serial EBV measurements, report reasons for missingness, and describe assay harmonization, detection thresholds, and quality control across 28 local laboratories.
- The EBV analyses are explicitly post hoc, involve multiple comparisons, and establish prognostic association rather than clinical utility. Statements that EBV DNA clearance should be incorporated into practice “to guide individualized treatment” or that nonclearance warrants alternative therapy are unsupported without prospective evidence that biomarker-guided treatment improves outcomes. Analyses comparing randomized groups within strata defined by postrandomization clearance are particularly difficult to interpret and should not be described as demonstrating treatment benefit irrespective of clearance without interaction testing and appropriate causal caveats.
- Analyses of patients completing 2 years of camrelizumab are dominated by immortal-time and responder-selection bias: patients must survive without progression long enough to complete treatment. A 5-year survival comparison from randomization cannot meaningfully evaluate treatment duration. This section and associated figure should either be removed or replaced by a clearly defined 2-year landmark analysis among patients alive and progression-free at that landmark, while retaining strong caution that treatment duration was not randomized.
- Comparisons of “5-year survivors” with those surviving less than 5 years are not clearly defined in the presence of censoring before 5 years and entail numerous unadjusted hypothesis tests in small selected groups. Please specify how censored patients were classified, avoid treating these analyses as identification of survivor characteristics, and consider presenting them descriptively without P values or removing them.
- Subsequent therapy requires reconciliation and more detailed interpretation. The Results report subsequent therapy in 61.2% vs 75.2% and PD-1/PD-L1 therapy in 29.9% vs 32.6%, whereas the Discussion cites different values (62/134 vs 87/129) to explain the baseline EBV-negative subgroup. These figures appear inconsistent with both the overall population and the stated reference to the EBV-negative subgroup. Correct the denominators and provide timing and class of subsequent therapies by randomized group, recognizing that postprotocol immunotherapy in the control group affects the treatment-policy OS estimand but does not explain subgroup results without appropriate analysis.
- The claim of a “survival plateau” is premature with follow-up only slightly beyond 5 years, limited numbers at risk, and continued censoring. The manuscript should describe the observed 5-year survival estimate without inferring a plateau unless substantially longer follow-up supports stabilization of the hazard.

MINOR CONCERNS:
- The efficacy population is termed intention-to-treat but defined as randomized patients receiving at least 1 dose, which is conventionally a modified intention-to-treat population. Because all randomized patients were treated, state that the true randomized population and treated population coincided.
- Clarify whether this analysis provides any updated safety findings after longer exposure and follow-up, or state explicitly that no updated safety analysis was performed.
- Generalizability should be framed more narrowly: all participants were Asian, all sites were in China, nearly all tumors were nonkeratinizing, ECOG status was 0 or 1, and all participants reportedly had distant metastases. The conclusions should not imply equivalent evidence for nonendemic, keratinizing, poor-performance-status, or locoregionally recurrent-only populations.
- The phrase “5-year OS benefit (HR, 0.74…)” conflates a time-to-event HR with the 5-year landmark contrast. Report the overall HR separately from the absolute 5-year difference.
- Report a treatment-by-baseline-EBV-status interaction P value rather than highlighting the null estimate in one underpowered subgroup.
- Ensure consistent terminology (“distant,” not “distal,” metastases; “conferred,” not “confered”) and consistent cutoff wording across the text and figure legends.
- The reference list and manuscript formatting contain several run-together citations and spacing errors, particularly references 8-9, 14-15, and 28-29.

DECISION: major_revision

**SUMMARY:**
This study applies normative modeling to graph-theoretical topological metrics derived from brain morphometric similarity networks (MSNs) in a multi-site discovery cohort of children with ADHD and typically developing controls. Using a semi-supervised clustering algorithm (HYDRA), the authors delineate three distinct ADHD biotypes characterized by unique neuroanatomical hub deviation patterns, clinical symptom profiles, spatial alignments with neurotransmitter density atlases, and cognitive meta-analytic maps. While external validation in an independent dataset (Healthy Brain Network) reproduced hyperactive/impulsive distinctions and topological profiles, inattentive profiles did not replicate across cohorts.

**MAJOR CONCERNS:**
- **Clustering Stability and Dimensionality:** The optimal clustering solution (k = 3) yielded an Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) of 0.21. Although statistically exceeding null permutations, an ARI of ~0.20 indicates modest stability with substantial overlap. The authors should temper claims of identifying discrete categorical "biotypes" versus capturing salient points along a shared dimensional spectrum, and discuss how low assignment stability affects individual-level clinical utility.
- **Partial Replication in Validation Cohort:** The external validation in the Healthy Brain Network cohort successfully reproduced between-biotype differences in hyperactivity/impulsivity but failed to replicate differences in inattention (P = .13 and P = .78 on CBCL). The Abstract and Conclusions should explicitly state that clinical validation was partial and domain-specific rather than presenting it as fully validated.
- **Modest Effect Sizes:** The effect sizes for clinical phenotype distinctions across biotypes (η² = 0.01–0.016) and case-control deviations (Cohen d = 0.12–0.17) are modest. The authors should explicitly discuss whether differences of this magnitude provide actionable clinical stratification for personalized interventions or risk prediction.
- **Interpretation of Spatial Neurotransmitter Contextualization:** Correlating biotype deviation topographies with adult PET-derived receptor density atlases is an indirect, ecological analysis. The manuscript should exercise caution in causal or mechanistic phrasing regarding neurochemical pathology in pediatric ADHD cohorts.

**MINOR CONCERNS:**
- **Harmonization and Site Effects:** Because discovery data aggregate multiple distinct scanning sites and protocols (including ABIDE and ADHD-200), more detail should be included in the main text explaining how multi-site scanner variance was handled during normative model training beyond the transfer learning framework used in validation.
- **Demographic Reporting:** In accordance with JAMA Network reporting guidelines, the omission of race and ethnicity data due to repository limitations should be formally noted in the Limitations section.
- **Figure and Text Callout Consistency:** Verify that text descriptions of subpanels in Figure 1 (e.g., panels D–H) match the figure caption labeling precisely.

DECISION: major_revision

SUMMARY: This randomized clinical trial tested a culturally and medically tailored meal program (MUTTON-HF) for heart failure patients in rural Navajo Nation. The intervention reduced the composite outcome of all-cause hospitalization or ED visit at 90 days compared to usual care (40.6% vs 57.0%; RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.54–0.96), with improvements in several secondary outcomes including weight, blood pressure, food insecurity, and KCCQ scores. The paper argues this is the first RCT of an Indigenous Food is Medicine intervention to show clinical benefit.

MAJOR CONCERNS:
- **Baseline imbalance in key prognostic factors:** Table 1 shows notable differences favoring the intervention arm, including lower rates of hypertension (64.2% vs 80.0%), atrial fibrillation (19.8% vs 24.0%), and CKD (31.1% vs 39.0%). These are strong predictors of hospitalization and ED use. The primary analysis is unadjusted; no multivariable models or sensitivity analyses are presented. Given the magnitude of these imbalances, the observed effect could be partly confounded. The authors should provide adjusted analyses (e.g., for hypertension, CKD, age, sex) or at least a discussion of the potential impact.
- **Open-label design and outcome ascertainment:** The trial was unblinded, and while EHR outcome extractors were masked, patients and clinicians were not. The primary outcome (hospitalization or ED visit) is objective but could be influenced by differential healthcare-seeking behavior or provider decisions. For example, intervention participants may have had more contact with study staff and thus more opportunity to avoid ED visits. The authors should explicitly address this risk and consider a sensitivity analysis using only adjudicated or EHR-confirmed events.
- **Confounding by appliance provision:** The intervention included not only meals but also microwaves, freezers, and propane-powered refrigerators for those lacking electricity. These infrastructure changes could independently improve food storage and preparation, thereby affecting health outcomes. The authors cannot attribute the effect solely to the meals. This should be acknowledged more prominently as a limitation, and the design precludes isolating the meal effect.
- **Sample size calculation and observed control event rate:** The trial was powered based on a hypothesized control event rate of 29%, but the observed control rate was 57%. This discrepancy suggests the baseline assumption was inaccurate, possibly because the eligibility criteria (prior hospitalization or ED visit) selected a much higher-risk population. The authors should explain why the control rate was so much higher than expected and discuss implications for generalizability and interpretation.
- **Missing data and multiple comparisons:** Missingness for surveys and laboratory data ranged from 8–14%. Complete-case analyses assume missing-at-random, but the authors note they cannot rule out differential missingness. Moreover, many secondary outcomes were tested without adjustment for multiple comparisons, increasing the risk of false positives. The authors should either present a prespecified hierarchy of secondary outcomes, apply a correction (e.g., Benjamini-Hochberg), or clearly label results as exploratory.
- **Adverse events not detailed:** The text states "There were significant differences in adverse events between arms" but does not describe what these events were or how they were classified. This is a critical safety outcome for a dietary intervention. The authors must report the types and severity of adverse events in the main text or at least summarize the most important findings.

MINOR CONCERNS:
- The analysis dates are listed as "December 2025 to February 2026," which appears to be in the future relative to the current date. Please verify and correct.
- The term "Fischer exact test" should be "Fisher exact test."
- The CONSORT diagram is referenced but not shown; it should be included as a figure.
- The paper would benefit from a CONSORT checklist to confirm reporting completeness.
- The authors use "KCCS" in the methods but later refer to "KCCQ" (Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire). Please use consistent terminology.
- The abstract states "Findings" with the primary outcome result, but it does not mention the baseline imbalance or the fact that the effect was driven by hospitalizations, which would be useful context.
- The trial is described as "pragmatic," but the intervention includes provision of appliances and propane, which is a complex and resource-intensive component. A brief description of the cost implications (beyond per-meal cost) would help readers assess scalability.

DECISION: major_revision

SUMMARY: This population-based Danish registry cohort study of 67,390 females with a first first-trimester abortion (2000–2018) examined whether medication vs procedural abortion was associated with first psychotropic medication redemption. Using pre-post comparisons within each abortion method, the authors report small increased risks in the year after abortion that do not survive Bonferroni correction, and decreased risks more than 5 years after abortion.

MAJOR CONCERNS:

1. **Absence of a comparison group is the fundamental design weakness.** The design compares post-abortion rates to pre-abortion rates within the same women. Without an unexposed (or differently exposed) comparison group, one cannot distinguish (a) an effect of abortion, (b) detection/access effects (as the authors themselves speculate regarding GP contact), or (c) secular trends and age-related changes in psychotropic prescribing. The authors' prior work included appropriate comparisons; the rationale for abandoning a comparison group here is not provided and should be. At minimum, a matched or population comparison would substantially strengthen causal interpretation.

2. **Confounding by indication and by the decision pathway.** Abortion method is strongly patterned by gestational age (87.8% of medication abortions <8 weeks vs 48.1% of procedural abortions at 9–11 weeks), and gestational age itself may relate to circumstances of the pregnancy, wantedness, and mental health. The fully adjusted model adjusts for gestational age, but gestational age is nearly collinear with method, making adjustment unstable and interpretation unclear. The sensitivity analysis restricted to 56–62 days is helpful but likely underpowered and selected; results should be reported with numbers at risk and event counts.

3. **Misclassification of exposure.** 2,500 women with both medication and procedural codes were classified as procedural, based on personal email communication. This is a nontrivial exposure misclassification (7% of the sample) justified only by unverifiable correspondence. Please document this decision more rigorously (e.g., citation to Danish register coding practice, sensitivity analyses already partially done) and discuss the likely direction of bias.

4. **The "decreased risk >5 years after" findings are difficult to interpret and may be artifactual.** A declining hazard of *first* psychotropic redemption with increasing time since abortion is expected under any frailty/selection structure (susceptible individuals redeem earlier), and the pre-period reference (the year immediately before abortion) may be a period of elevated help-seeking or distress. The authors should explicitly address regression to the mean and time-on-study biases; the framing of "decreased risk" as a substantive finding risks misleading readers.

5. **The exclusion of 15,932 women with psychotropic redemptions more than 1 year before the abortion** introduces survivorship/selection bias: the analytic sample is conditioned on being psychotropic-free for an extended pre-abortion period, which interacts with the first-event outcome. Discuss how this affects generalizability and the pre-post contrast.

6. **Inconsistency in narrative vs results.** The Key Points/abstract state there was "no increased risk... between 2 to 5 years," yet the fully adjusted model shows a significantly increased risk of antianxiety medication redemption 2–5 years after medication abortion (IRR, 1.26) that survives Bonferroni correction. This discrepancy between abstract and results must be reconciled; the abstract as written misrepresents the findings.

7. **Multiple testing strategy.** The Bonferroni correction divides by 24 for the first analysis set and 11 for the second, but the total family of tests across all outcomes, methods, time windows, and models is far larger. Conversely, the paper toggles between conventional and corrected thresholds in a way that risks selective interpretation. Pre-specify a coherent inference framework (e.g., report all estimates with CIs and emphasize effect sizes and precision rather than threshold-crossing).

MINOR CONCERNS:

- Table 3 footnote describes covariates as "mother's and father's psychotropic drug use" whereas the Methods describe parental *psychiatric diagnoses*; reconcile.
- Table 2: the incidence rate for "any psychiatric diagnosis: Yes" appears misaligned across outcome columns (53.3 for antidepressants seems inconsistent with 23.9); verify.
- "9-12 wk" appears in Table 2 where Methods say 9–11 weeks.
- Age categories sum to 100.1% (19.7 + 80.4); check.
- The Poisson model "approximating a Cox regression model" needs clearer justification; also clarify how time-varying calendar year was modeled within intervals.
- The rationale for bimonthly (2-month) bins and the choice of months 11–12 before abortion as reference should be justified; results may be sensitive to binning.
- The Discussion would benefit from discussing residual confounding (e.g., pregnancy intention, intimate partner violence, socioeconomic adversity at time of pregnancy) rather than only detection effects.
- "Females" vs "women" used inconsistently.
- The claim in the Limitations that "the claim that medication abortion harms mental health is universal for all contexts" is an overstatement; rephrase.
- Consider reporting absolute risk differences alongside IRRs; IRRs of 1.08–1.26 on modest base rates correspond to small absolute differences that are more interpretable for clinical readers.

DECISION: major_revision

SUMMARY: This population-based SEER study reports that 1-year cause-specific survival among patients diagnosed with cancer in 2020 and 2021 was lower than survival extrapolated from 2015-2019 trends, including within broadly defined early- and late-stage groups. The authors attribute these differences to pandemic-related disruptions and estimate 17 390 more cancer deaths within 1 year of diagnosis than expected.

MAJOR CONCERNS:
- The design does not support the causal interpretation that pandemic-related care disruptions produced the observed survival differences or 17 390 “additional” deaths. This is an uncontrolled extrapolation from only 5 prepandemic annual observations, and any slowing of prior survival improvement would appear as a pandemic deficit. The manuscript should consistently describe associations, substantially temper claims regarding deaths “that would have occurred” absent the pandemic, and consider alternative counterfactual models and baseline periods, including a no-trend comparison with 2019.
- Case-mix changes are insufficiently addressed. Stage stratification alone does not control for changes in cancer-site distribution, age, comorbidity, histology, grade, molecular subtype, or extent of disease within the very broad localized and regional/distant categories. This is particularly problematic for the all-cancer analysis, where changes in the proportions of cancers with markedly different prognoses could generate an apparent survival change. Individual-level, standardized or adjusted analyses are needed, along with finer stage categories and site-specific adjustment where feasible.
- Conditioning on cancers diagnosed during the pandemic creates substantial selection concerns. Screening interruptions and underdiagnosis altered which patients entered the diagnosed cohort; stage adjustment cannot eliminate within-stage changes in symptom burden, tumor biology, or lead time. Excluding unknown-stage cases may further bias results if staging completeness changed during the pandemic. The authors should quantify temporal changes in unknown stage and other exclusions, perform sensitivity analyses, and clarify that these estimates do not measure the total population mortality consequences of missed cancers.
- The derivation and interpretation of the mortality difference are unclear and potentially invalid. The authors multiply survival differences by incidence rates and a fixed “standard US population” of 274 633 642, using exactly half that population for sex-specific cancers, despite SEER covering 41.9% of the population. Age-standardized incidence rates multiplied by a standard population do not necessarily yield actual national death counts. The manuscript must provide complete formulas, identify whether rates are crude or age adjusted, explain the population denominator and national extrapolation, propagate all sources of uncertainty, and reconcile the estimate with the observed SEER case and death counts. Unless this approach can be validated, the result should be presented as a standardized model-based quantity rather than a count of US excess deaths.
- Cause-specific survival depends on cause-of-death classification, which may have changed during COVID-19. Censoring deaths attributed to COVID-19 can also yield a selected risk set and does not necessarily isolate disruptions in cancer care. The finding that relative-survival reductions were larger does not by itself exclude misclassification or pandemic-related competing-risk effects, especially given acknowledged limitations of pandemic life tables. Results for overall survival, cancer-specific cumulative incidence with competing risks, cause-specific survival, and relative survival should be presented together and interpreted cautiously.
- The statistical methods require substantially more detail and validation. With only 5 annual prepandemic estimates, model selection and extrapolation uncertainty are consequential. The authors should report fitted models, goodness of fit, assumptions, prediction intervals, and sensitivity to alternative trend specifications. It is also unclear whether confidence intervals for observed-minus-expected survival fully include uncertainty in the expected values. Numerous subgroup and site-stage comparisons are made using pointwise significance without multiplicity control; these should be identified as exploratory or addressed analytically.
- The manuscript defines 1-year CSS as the number alive at 1 year divided by the number diagnosed, but the actuarial cause-specific survival estimator is not a simple proportion when censoring and competing deaths occur. The estimand, censoring rules, handling of loss to follow-up, and actuarial interval construction should be stated accurately. Given 63 967 patients reportedly lost to follow-up, sensitivity to differential censoring by diagnosis year is important.

MINOR CONCERNS:
- The 2020 late-stage CSS is reported as 74.78% in the text, whereas Table 2 and its confidence interval indicate 74.18%.
- The text reports 341 additional brain cancer deaths with a 95% CI of 98-148, which is incompatible with both the point estimate and Table 3 (148-533).
- Table 1 percentages for deaths appear to represent the distribution of all deaths across categories rather than mortality within each category; column headings or footnotes should make this explicit.
- Figure 2 contains the wording “number of patients are risk,” which should be “number of patients at risk.”
- “Other non-Hispanic race” combines Asian or Pacific Islander and American Indian or Alaska Native populations despite different cancer patterns and pandemic experiences. Analyses should be separated where sample sizes permit, and conclusions about this heterogeneous group should be restrained.
- The rationale for the selected cancer categories is partly subjective (“approximately” one-third or two-thirds survival). Prespecified numeric thresholds and the precise source year should be provided.
- References and dates require verification, particularly reference 9 and the software update/access dates.

DECISION: major_revision

**SUMMARY:**
This large retrospective cohort study uses federated electronic health record data (TriNetX) across 62 US health care organizations to map 2-year risks of 14 psychiatric and neurologic disorders following hospitalization with infections across 10 body systems compared to non-infectious hospitalized controls, the general population, and head-to-head across infection types. The authors demonstrate that post-infectious psychiatric and neurologic risks are broadly elevated across systems, with relative risk highest for encephalitis and absolute risk increase highest for cognitive deficits. Furthermore, absolute risk increases followed an ascending age gradient (lowest in children, highest in older adults), and hierarchical clustering revealed distinct shared-risk profiles among psychiatric and neurologic sequelae.

**MAJOR CONCERNS:**
- None. This is an exceptionally well-executed, comprehensive, and methodologically rigorous study addressing a major clinical and public health question using robust statistical methods (propensity score matching across 92 covariates, restricted mean time lost ratio analysis, network meta-analysis, and clustering).

**MINOR CONCERNS:**
- *Surveillance and Detection Bias:* Individuals hospitalized with severe infections may undergo more frequent medical follow-up or diagnostic workups than general outpatient controls or certain non-infectious hospitalized controls, potentially leading to differential ascertainment of subtle cognitive, mood, or neurological disorders. While the 30-day post-acute buffer and hospitalized control group mitigate this, a brief mention of potential surveillance/ascertainment bias in the Limitations section would strengthen the discussion.
- *Definition of Cognitive Deficits:* "Cognitive deficits" is reported as a composite outcome; it would be helpful to briefly clarify in the main text methods which primary diagnostic categories/ICD-10 codes comprise this composite (e.g., mild cognitive impairment, unspecified cognitive decline) to aid clinical interpretability without requiring cross-referencing to the supplement.
- *Handling of Competing Risks (Mortality):* Given the 2-year follow-up and inclusion of an older adult population hospitalized with severe infections, non-neurological/non-psychiatric mortality represents a competing risk. While RMTL accounts well for non-proportional hazards, a brief comment on how mortality was treated or whether it could influence follow-up duration across older cohorts would be informative.

DECISION: accept

SUMMARY: This population-based cohort study using SEER-21 data compares 1-year cause-specific survival for patients diagnosed with cancer in 2020–2021 to expected survival based on 2015–2019 trends. The authors report significant reductions in survival for both early- and late-stage disease, translating to an estimated 17,390 excess cancer deaths within 1 year of diagnosis, with the largest impacts in older adults and certain racial/ethnic groups.

MAJOR CONCERNS:
- **Confounding by case mix**: The study does not adequately address potential changes in tumor severity within stage categories resulting from pandemic-related underdiagnosis. Stratification by stage may not capture shifts in histology, grade, or symptom status. The authors should perform sensitivity analyses adjusting for additional tumor characteristics (e.g., grade, histology) or discuss the magnitude of this bias more explicitly. Without such analyses, the observed survival reductions could partly reflect a change in the composition of diagnosed cases rather than a true decline in care quality.
- **Multiple testing**: The authors test many subgroups and cancer sites without any adjustment for multiple comparisons. This inflates the risk of false-positive findings, particularly for site-specific and subgroup analyses. They should apply a correction (e.g., false discovery rate) or at least acknowledge this limitation and interpret borderline results cautiously.
- **Mortality difference estimation**: The method of multiplying the absolute survival difference by the observed number of cases is an approximation that may be biased because cause-specific survival is not an additive measure. A more rigorous approach would directly model observed vs. expected deaths using individual-level data. Additionally, the authors do not provide a combined confidence interval for the total 17,390 excess deaths; they should present a single estimate with uncertainty for the overall impact.
- **Model validation**: The expected survival rates are derived from proportional hazards models fit to 2015–2019 data. The authors should provide details on model fit, the linearity assumption of the trend, and demonstrate that the extrapolation to 2020–2021 is robust (e.g., by back-testing on 2019 data). Without this, the “expected” rates may be unreliable.

MINOR CONCERNS:
- In Table 2, the observed CSS for late-stage 2020 is listed as 74.78% but the 95% CI is 74.00–74.35%, which is inconsistent; likely a typo for 74.18%.
- In the Results section, the CI for brain cancer deaths is incorrectly written as “98-148” instead of “148-533” (as in Table 3).
- Reference 9 appears to cite a journal abbreviated as “OOR” which seems erroneous; please verify.
- The authors state the dataset was assembled 22 months after the latest follow-up date, but they do not specify the actual follow-up date. Please clarify.
- Figure legends contain typos: “patients are risk” should be “patients at risk”.
- The reference to SEER*Stat software includes future dates (accessed January 21, 2026); please correct.

DECISION: major_revision

SUMMARY: The authors use the TriNetX US EHR network to compare risks of 14 psychiatric and neurologic disorders in the 1 month to 2 years after hospitalization for infections across 10 body systems, versus hospitalized noninfectious controls, the general population, and each other, stratified by age. They report broadly elevated postinfection risks, with infectious encephalitides as the leading relative risk factor for most disorders, cognitive deficits showing the largest absolute excess, and an age gradient in absolute risks.

MAJOR CONCERNS:
1. **Residual confounding and the limits of propensity matching.** Despite matching on 92 covariates, the fundamental problem remains: individuals hospitalized with infections differ systematically from those hospitalized for other causes (and from the general population) in ways EHR data cannot capture—frailty, alcohol/substance use, socioeconomic adversity, healthcare-seeking patterns, and baseline neuropsychiatric vulnerability. Infection hospitalization is largely a marker of being unwell. The authors acknowledge this but the Discussion at times drifts toward causal/mechanistic language ("risks remain after extensive adjustment," pandemic preparedness claims) that the design cannot support. The paper would benefit from a more consistent framing of associations as hypothesis-generating, and ideally a sensitivity analysis (e.g., E-value or negative-control outcomes).

2. **Confounding by indication and severity is not addressed between infection cohorts.** Head-to-head comparisons between infections implicitly assume that, after matching, the only difference is infection type—but severity of illness, ICU admission, length of stay, and delirium differ enormously across infection types (e.g., encephalitides vs skin infections). The authors note they did not assess mediation by acute complications, yet these are more plausibly confounders than mediators in this design. This is particularly problematic for the headline finding that infectious encephalitides are the leading risk factor for most disorders, since encephalitis hospitalizations are by definition neurologically ill.

3. **Circularity in the encephalitis outcome.** Encephalitis as an *outcome* after infections—including after non-CNS infections—is difficult to interpret. The 30-day washout may not fully exclude index misdiagnosis, and the outcome includes "infectious and noninfectious" encephalitis, meaning the same condition could plausibly be part of the index illness trajectory. This deserves more than a brief caveat; a sensitivity analysis excluding infectious encephalitis as an outcome, or extending the washout, is needed.

4. **The STI–psychosis/mood/dementia association is likely driven by HIV.** The authors themselves note HIV was the leading STI in older groups and that HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder is coded under dementia. But HIV infection also confounds the psychosis and mood findings (HIV-associated psychosis, substance use comorbidity). A sensitivity analysis excluding HIV-positive patients from the STI cohort is warranted before these associations are presented as infection-specific.

5. **Competing risk of death is not handled.** In older adults—where absolute risks are highest—death is a strong competing event. KM cumulative incidence overstates risk in the presence of competing mortality, and the RMTL "time lost" interpretation conflates time lost to death with time spent with the disorder. Please clarify the estimand or use competing-risk methods (Fine-Gray or cause-specific RMTL decomposition).

6. **Cohort overlap.** Individuals can appear in multiple infection cohorts and as controls, and TriNetX prevents deduplication. The claim that overlap was "small" (eResults 2) needs quantification in the main text, and the authors should discuss correlated estimates in the network meta-analysis, which assumes independence.

7. **Misclassification of exposure and outcomes.** Admission-day ICD codes as the exposure definition is coarse; "hospitalization with an infection" vs "for an infection" is not distinguishable, and the authors appropriately hedge. But outcome ascertainment via billing codes for conditions like cognitive deficits, insomnia, and anxiety is highly sensitive to care-contact patterns—infected patients have far more follow-up contacts, creating detection bias that inflates apparent risk. This should be discussed explicitly and, if possible, addressed (e.g., restricting to patients with equivalent visit frequency during follow-up).

MINOR CONCERNS:
- Statistical analysis period "May 2024 to March 2026" — please correct the dates.
- Mixed multiplicity correction (Bonferroni for infection-control comparisons, Benjamini-Hochberg for age moderation, Bonferroni for the correlation matrix, apparently uncorrected for the 45 head-to-head comparisons) is inconsistent; justify or harmonize.
- The "92 confounders" claim should be tempered—many are ICD-coded comorbidity indicators; the effective confounding control is far weaker than the number implies.
- The pandemic-preparedness claim (predicting COVID-19 sequelae from RTI patterns) is post hoc and overstated; the cited COVID literature was available when this analysis was designed. Soften.
- The "brain-muscle signaling axis" speculation in the Discussion is too speculative for this journal; trim.
- Figure 2: please define in the legend how the median RMTL ratio color was computed (vs all other infections—i.e., a summary of 9 comparisons?).
- Children's STI cohort (mean age 15.6) raises questions about coding of abuse-related infections; consider a comment.
- "Risk map"/"atlas" language: ensure consistent terminology and that conclusions avoid implying clinical decision rules are validated.
- Abstract should state the observational, association-only nature of the findings more prominently.

DECISION: major_revision

**Reviewer Report**

**Summary**

This retrospective cohort study using the multi-institutional NCC LungReal database examines whether adherence to two lymph node dissection (LND) guidelines (the 3+1 standard and the more stringent 6-station standard) is associated with overall survival (OS) in patients with clinical T1N0M0 lung adenocarcinoma, stratified by histologic pattern (lepidic with no high-grade [LepNH] vs. high-grade or no lepidic [HGNL]). The authors report that guideline-adherent LND was associated with improved OS in the HGNL group, particularly for larger tumors, but not in the LepNH group, where survival was excellent regardless of LND extent. They conclude that LND guidelines should be selectively applied based on histologic pattern, pending prospective validation.

**Major Concerns**

1. **Incomplete Manuscript**: The submitted text is heavily truncated with numerous ellipses (“[…]”) replacing critical sections, including detailed methods, statistical analyses, results tables, and figure legends. Key data (e.g., full patient characteristics, hazard ratios with confidence intervals, exact numbers of events) are missing. This makes it impossible to fully assess the validity of the analyses or the robustness of the conclusions. A complete manuscript is required for proper peer review.

2. **Observational Design and Residual Confounding**: The study is retrospective and non-randomized. Although the authors mention statistical adjustment, the specific variables included in the multivariable models are not fully described. Unmeasured confounders (e.g., surgeon experience, intraoperative findings, patient comorbidity burden, pulmonary function, adjuvant therapy receipt) could influence both the extent of LND and OS. The decision to perform a more limited LND may be driven by technical difficulties or patient frailty, biasing results toward a survival benefit for more extensive dissection. Propensity score matching or instrumental variable analysis would strengthen causal inference, but these are not mentioned.

3. **Selection Bias and Immortal Time Bias**: Patients who underwent more extensive LND may have had better baseline performance status or more favorable anatomy. Conversely, those with limited dissection might have had intraoperative complications or unexpected findings that led to abbreviated surgery. The timing of LND relative to surgery and follow-up is not clarified, raising the possibility of immortal time bias if survival is measured from a time point after the LND decision.

4. **Sparse Events and Exploratory Subgroup Analyses**: The authors acknowledge low events per variable (EPV) in several subgroups, particularly in the LepNH group and the 1-cm or smaller HGNL subgroups. For example, the 6-station standard adherence analysis in the LepNH group had only 0.54 HR with a wide confidence interval (P = .10). Many subgroup analyses are underpowered, and the authors appropriately label them as exploratory; however, drawing clinical conclusions from these underpowered estimates is risky. The multiple comparisons across histologic groups, size strata, and two LND standards increase the risk of type I error, and no correction for multiple testing is described.

5. **Histologic Pattern Assessment**: The classification into LepNH vs. HGNL relies on postoperative pathology, but the authors discuss intraoperative frozen section sensitivity (37%–69%) for high-grade patterns. This implies that many HGNL tumors would be misclassified as LepNH during surgery, undermining the practical applicability of selective LND based on frozen section. The manuscript does not provide a strategy to overcome this limitation, nor does it analyze outcomes based on intraoperative assessment.

6. **Lack of Recurrence Data**: The study uses OS as the primary endpoint, but for early-stage lung cancer, disease-free survival or recurrence is a more sensitive outcome. The authors note that recurrence data were unavailable. Given the excellent OS in the LepNH group, any potential harm or benefit of LND on recurrence cannot be assessed, and OS may be influenced by non-cancer deaths and subsequent treatments.

7. **Generalizability and Database Completeness**: The NCC LungReal database appears to be a voluntary, multi-institutional registry. The completeness of nodal station data, the accuracy of pathologic staging, and the representativeness of the participating centers are not described. The study period (2014–2021) includes changes in surgical techniques (e.g., video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery) and adjuvant therapy indications, which are not accounted for.

8. **Presentation of Results**: The manuscript is poorly organized due to the truncation, but even within the readable portions, the results are presented in a fragmented manner. Tables and figures are referenced but not fully provided. The Kaplan-Meier curves and forest plots are not shown, making it difficult to evaluate the proportional hazards assumption or the shape of survival curves.

**Minor Concerns**

- The introduction is repetitive, with several sentences duplicated (e.g., the rationale for histologic subtyping is stated multiple times). The text should be streamlined.
- The term “LepNH” and “HGNL” are used before full definitions are provided in the methods; ensure clear definition at first use.
- The authors state that “adherence with the 6-station standard” was associated with better survival in the HGNL group, but the comparison is against “adherent solely with the 3+1 standard.” This exploratory analysis should be clearly described and justified, as it directly compares two different adherent groups rather than adherent vs. non-adherent.
- The discussion of the immune role of lymph nodes (refs 20,21) is speculative and not directly supported by the data; it should be toned down.
- The conclusions are appropriately cautious, but the abstract states “lymph node dissection adherent with the 3+1 or 6-station standard was associated with survival benefit” in the HGNL group, which may overstate the observational evidence given the aforementioned limitations.
- The manuscript would benefit from sensitivity analyses excluding patients with less than a certain number of nodes examined, or using alternative definitions of “adherent” (e.g., number of N2 stations, total nodes removed).
- The authors should report the median number of nodes removed in each group and the distribution of stations sampled to ensure that the “non-adherent” group is not simply a group with very limited sampling.

**Decision**

The manuscript addresses an important clinical question with a large, real-world dataset. However, the incomplete submission, substantial methodological limitations, and sparse events in key subgroups prevent acceptance in its current form. The authors need to provide a complete manuscript, address confounding and selection bias more rigorously, and temper conclusions given the observational nature and exploratory analyses. I recommend **major revision** before reconsideration.

DECISION: major_revision

SUMMARY: The authors apply normative modeling to topological metrics (degree centrality, nodal efficiency, participation coefficient) derived from individual morphometric similarity networks in a large multisite pediatric ADHD sample (~446 cases, 708 controls; 554 cases, 123 controls for validation). They identify three data-driven "biotypes" via HYDRA clustering of deviation maps, characterize clinical profiles, longitudinal trajectories, neurotransmitter receptor spatial correlations, and Neurosynth cognitive associations, and report partial replication in an independent Healthy Brain Network cohort.

MAJOR CONCERNS:

1. **Effect sizes are very small relative to the framing.** Case-control differences in extreme deviations are d = 0.12–0.17, and the mCCA+jICA group differences are d ≈ 0.13–0.15. With ~95% of ADHD children showing at least one extreme deviation (and TDCs showing nearly as many: 4.19 vs 4.54 deviations), the normative deviation approach captures largely nonspecific variation. The abstract and discussion should be tempered accordingly; the claim of "robust stratification biomarkers" is not supported by these effect sizes.

2. **Clustering stability is weak.** Adjusted Rand indices of 0.21 (k=3) vs 0.18 (k=2) vs 0.17 (k=4) provide little evidence that k=3 is a genuinely superior solution; these differences are marginal and the absolute stability is low. The authors should report formal statistical comparisons across k and discuss how fragile the 3-biotype solution is. The claim that k=3 "best captured heterogeneity" overstates the evidence.

3. **Potential circularity in "biological validation" of clinical profiles.** The claim that neuroimaging-derived clusters "converged with clinical phenotypes without using any clinical features" and thereby "biologically validate" DSM presentations is overstated. The clinical differences between biotypes are small (η² ≈ 0.01–0.02), largely driven by severity gradients (biotype 1 is simply the most severe on most measures), and the inattention distinction did not replicate in the validation cohort. A severity-only interpretation should be explicitly considered as an alternative to the proposed distinct-mechanism account.

4. **Validation cohort replication is only partial.** Hyperactivity/impulsivity differences replicated weakly (P = .04, d small), but inattention did not (P = .13; CBCL attention P = .78). The discussion attributes this to age, recruitment, and "cross-cultural variations," but this is speculative; the honest conclusion is that the biotype clinical signatures are not robustly reproducible.

5. **Confounding and sample characterization.** Medication status at scan is not reported for the discovery sample (only addressed in the longitudinal subsample), IQ and comorbidity handling need clearer description, and site/scanner effects—despite the SVM site-prediction check—should be shown to not drive the deviation maps (e.g., ComBat-harmonized sensitivity analyses). The markedly different sex ratios across groups (24% female in ADHD vs 39% in TDC) and across sites also warrant sensitivity analyses beyond the brief male-only check.

6. **Neurotransmitter and Neurosynth analyses are exploratory and should not be framed as validation.** Spatial correlations with PET receptor maps (r = 0.24–0.41) are hypothesis-generating; the authors appropriately caveat this in one sentence but the Conclusion ("spatial molecular signatures... with rigorous validation") contradicts it. Similarly, Neurosynth decoding with spin P values of .04–.048 is weak evidence. The title/abstract/conclusion language should be revised.

7. **MSN interpretability.** The authors acknowledge that morphometric similarity networks are correlation-based and not directly interpretable as connections; yet the discussion repeatedly invokes "connector hubs," "compensatory adaptation," and "frontostriatal circuitry" in mechanistic terms. Graph-theoretic language (degree, participation coefficient) applied to similarity networks requires consistent hedging throughout.

8. **Multiple testing and threshold choices.** The |z| ≥ 2 threshold, uncorrected P < .05 for nodal χ² tests, and 19 receptor × 3 biotype correlation matrix need clearer multiplicity control; several reported findings sit at FDR P ≈ .03–.05.

MINOR CONCERNS:

- Figure 1 legend references panels B–H but the described pipeline (e.g., "Figure 1F," "Figure 1H") does not match the actual panels; check consistency.
- "Volumetric patterns of brain gray matter were exacted" — should be "extracted."
- eFigure 13 title typo: "HYDRA Mode."
- Reporting inconsistency: "339 male [76.0%]" vs "279 female [39.4%]" — percentages should be checked.
- "although without statistical significance" in the mood disorder sentence is grammatically redundant ("although... although").
- The Kruskal-Wallis statistic H and η² should be accompanied by df and effect-size definitions.
- The claim that biotype naming ("severe-combined with emotional dysregulation," etc.) is data-driven should be softened—these labels embed clinical interpretation.
- References 12 and 29 are preprints; consider whether peer-reviewed versions exist.
- STROBE guideline citation is appropriate, but a checklist should be included.

DECISION: major_revision

SUMMARY:
This manuscript presents an elegant and rigorous experimental evolution framework that "replays" germinal center (GC) reactions over 100 times using a monoclonal B cell system (clone 2.1 specific for chicken IgY). By integrating deep mutational scanning (DMS), passenger allele mutation profiles, single-cell BCR phylogenetics, cryo-EM structural biology, and mathematical modeling, the authors quantify the GC affinity-fitness landscape and reconcile long-standing paradoxes regarding GC permissiveness and clonal bursts. Notably, the study demonstrates that apparent early affinity plateaus and tolerance of low-affinity clones are primarily driven by macroevolutionary survivorship biases ("push-of-the-past" and "pull-of-the-present") rather than fundamental shifts in selective stringency.

MAJOR CONCERNS:
None. The experimental design is exceptionally thorough, the datasets are robust and multifaceted, and the mathematical framework convincingly supports the conclusions.

MINOR CONCERNS:
1. **Epistasis at High Mutation Loads:** The additive model for predicting variant affinity performs remarkably well for clone 2.1 across the tested BLI panel (mostly 1–3 mutations). However, at extended time points (e.g., 70 dpi, where mutation loads reach up to 37 mutations), higher-order epistatic interactions might become non-negligible. While the authors appropriately discuss epistasis in the context of bNAbs, adding a brief sentence discussing whether higher mutational loads at late time points might deviate from strict additivity would further strengthen the Discussion.
2. **Impact of Differentiation/Egress on Extinction Probabilities:** In the stochastic birth-death-mutation master equation (Equation 3), lineage "death" (μ(t)) functionally encompasses both apoptosis and differentiation into long-lived plasma cells or memory B cells (which permanently exit the active GC pool). Clarifying in the text how cellular differentiation/egress is incorporated or abstracted into the effective death rate would be helpful for non-specialist readers.
3. **Typography and Special Characters:** In several places in the text and table captions, special characters appear corrupted or improperly rendered (e.g., "√ó" instead of "×", "Œî" instead of "Δ", "œÅ" instead of "ρ", "Œ∫" instead of "κ"). Please ensure standard mathematical and Greek symbols are properly formatted in the final production files.
4. **Interactive Resources and Data Access:** The inclusion of public GitHub and interactive visualization links is commendable. Please ensure all repository links and PDB/EMDB accession codes (such as those referenced in Table S1/Figure 2) are finalized and publicly unlocked prior to final publication.

DECISION: minor_revision

SUMMARY: This Danish registry study compares rates of first psychotropic medication redemption after a first-trimester medication or procedural abortion with rates during the year before that abortion. The authors report small increases during the first postabortion year that generally do not meet a Bonferroni-adjusted significance threshold, along with lower rates more than 5 years later, and conclude that the findings do not support increased mental health risk after abortion.

MAJOR CONCERNS:
- The design cannot establish whether abortion is associated with the outcome. All participants had an abortion, and postabortion rates are compared only with the preceding year. This comparison cannot distinguish an abortion-related change from aging, secular prescribing trends, pregnancy-related changes, health care contact, or the underlying mental health trajectory that may precede an abortion. Adjustment for calendar year and age at abortion does not address attained age or these time-varying factors. A suitable comparison group and clearly specified target estimand would be required to support the manuscript’s central claim.
- Comparing first-event rates over successive intervals creates substantial risk-set depletion. Individuals redeeming medication before abortion cease follow-up and cannot contribute postabortion events; individuals redeeming medication shortly afterward similarly cannot remain at risk in later periods. Consequently, the progressively selected event-free group will tend to have lower long-term incidence even without a protective association. The reported reductions after 5 years are therefore not interpretable as evidence of reduced risk, and the analysis needs survival methods using attained age/time scales and an appropriate external comparison group.
- The analytic approach and variance estimation are insufficiently described. If records were split across time intervals for Poisson regression, the authors should specify the person-period construction, baseline hazard parameterization, treatment of within-person dependence, and use of robust standard errors. It is also unclear how “time-varying calendar year” was operationalized and whether the antidepressant and antianxiety analyses censored participants after redemption of another psychotropic class. Subsequent abortions are not addressed.
